messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About DIC help.-
parts:
We output the unnormalized log joint log probability
with each draw. But not the log likelihood.

To calculate DIC with Stan, you'd need to
define the log likelihood as a generated quantity
and then compute DIC on the outside of Stan itself
once you have the log likelihood for each draw.

Depending on the demand for DIC-like calcs, we may make
it easier by allowing the model to specified explicitly
in terms of a prior block and a log likelihood block so that
we could output the log likelihood without the user having
to essentially define the model twice.

- Bob

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About DIC help.-
parts:
I'm attaching a working DIC computation example, comparing a multilevel model to a fixed model using DIC (reduces to AIC in fixed case). The deviance is calculated in the generated quantities block. Then I compute the expected parameter values outside of Stan and manually compute the deviance at the expectations.

All Stan would really need to do to make this easy would be provide for a final calculation of generated quantities at the expected values of the trace. But that would just be a convenience.

I'm personally torn on whether software should make these metrics easy or not. On the one hand, all of these metrics (DIC/WAIC) are flawed. On the other hand, ignoring over fitting can be worse.

> I'm attaching a working DIC computation example, comparing a multilevel model to a fixed model using DIC (reduces to AIC

> the expected values of the trace. But that would just be a convenience.
>
> I'm personally torn on whether software should make these metrics easy or not. On the one hand, all of these metrics
> (DIC/WAIC) are flawed. On the other hand, ignoring over fitting can be worse.

I have no opinion on DIC.

The reason we can't automate the calculation of
the log likelihood is that the Stan model isn't
neatly divided into a likelihood and prior component.

If we split the model into two blocks, then we could
calculate the log likelihood (and log prior and log joint)
without measurable extra cost and without extra code in the generated
quantities block.

I believe our jury (i.e., Andrew) is still out on what
to do, so we've been holding off building in that kind of
thing.

One issue on the horizon is that we're imagining writing
compound models that have priors and likelihood in one
function call. That would get in the way of splitting out
the likelihood calc unless we did something fancier.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: [stan-users] DIC talk
parts:
I'm not thrilled with DIC but I don't know if we have any better alternatives right now. There are 3 difficulties with computing DIC in Stan. The first, as Bob noted, is that to compute DIC, the user would need to flag which parts of the unnormalized joint density go into the "likelihood." There's no automatic way of doing this; it depends not just on the model but on the purposes for which it will be used. But, not only is there no automatic way to identify these lines of code, in Stan there's no way to do it by hand. This is the problem Bob was pointing out: we would have to alter Stan to allow the user to flag the appropriate lines in the code. The third difficulty with implementing DIC is that it requires computation of the log likelihood given the posterior mean of the parameters. This requires computation of the mean and feeding it back into the calculation (also it requires some help if the likelihood is undefined at the posterior mean of theta, which in turn is one reason I'm not thrilled with DIC.

A
